questions.question: What does useRef return?
options: A state value and a setter
A mutable object with a current property that React preserves between renders
A DOM node directly
A memoised callback
questions.explanation: `useRef` returns the same `{ current }` object on every render. You mutate `current` freely, and React never re-renders because of it.

questions.question: What happens when you change ref.current?
options: React re-renders the component
The value changes with no re-render scheduled
React throws an error for mutating during render
The ref object is replaced
questions.explanation: Ref mutations are invisible to React's rendering. That is the point: it is storage, not state.

questions.question: Which value is best kept in a ref rather than state?
options: The text shown in a heading
A validation error the user must see
A timeout id used only for cleanup
Whether a modal is open
questions.explanation: A timeout id must survive renders but never appears on screen. Anything the UI displays belongs in state.

questions.question: Why is inputRef.current null during the first render?
options: Refs are always null in function components
The DOM node does not exist until React commits the render
You must call useRef twice
The ref attribute was misspelled
questions.explanation: React attaches the node after committing, so the ref is only populated by the time effects and event handlers run.

questions.question: Which of these is a poor use of a DOM ref?
options: Calling focus() on an input
Measuring an element with getBoundingClientRect
Setting an element's text content directly
Calling play() on a video
questions.explanation: Writing content or classes by hand fights React, which will overwrite it on the next render. Refs are for imperative browser APIs, not for rendering.

questions.question: What problem does forwardRef solve?
options: It makes refs re-render the component
It lets a ref placed on a custom component reach a DOM node inside it
It converts a ref into state
It creates refs in a loop
questions.explanation: `ref` is not a normal prop in React 18 and below, so a component must explicitly forward it to the element the parent should reach.

questions.question: What does useImperativeHandle do?
options: Replaces useEffect for imperative code
Chooses what the parent's ref.current will contain
Forces a re-render from a ref
Attaches multiple refs to one node
questions.explanation: It lets a component expose a small, deliberate API - such as play and pause - instead of handing the parent the raw DOM node.
